slot.topic_title: Justifying a Claim Based on a Confidence Interval for the Difference Between Two Population Means

item.title: Using an Interval to Judge Claims About Two Teaching Methods
item.stimulus: A school district randomly assigns 120 students to learn a unit with Method A and 120 students to learn it with Method B. Each student takes the same end-of-unit exam, scored out of 100. Let μA − μB be the true difference in mean exam score (Method A minus Method B). A 95% confidence interval for μA − μB is (2.1, 9.7) points. The conditions for the interval were met.

parts.prompt: Does the interval provide convincing evidence of a difference in mean exam score between the two methods? If so, state which method has the higher mean, and explain.

criteria.text: States that the interval provides convincing evidence of a difference, because 0 is not in the interval.
criteria.evidence: Response concludes there is convincing evidence of a difference and cites that 0 is not in (2.1, 9.7).
criteria.fix: If 0 is outside the interval, state that 0 is not a plausible value and so there is convincing evidence of a difference.

criteria.text: States that Method A has the higher mean score, because every value in the interval is positive for A minus B.
criteria.evidence: Response identifies Method A as having the higher mean and ties it to all values in the interval being positive.
criteria.fix: Use the order of subtraction: all values of A minus B positive means the mean for A is higher.

parts.prompt: A school board member claims that the true mean difference is exactly 5 points. Is the claim consistent with the interval? Does the interval establish that the claim is true? Explain.

criteria.text: States that the claim is consistent with the interval, because 5 is in the interval (2.1, 9.7) and so is a plausible value.
criteria.evidence: Response states 5 lies inside the interval and is a plausible value for the difference.
criteria.fix: Check whether the claimed value lies between the limits; if it does, the interval is consistent with the claim.

criteria.text: States that the interval does not establish that the difference is exactly 5, because other values in the interval are also plausible.
criteria.evidence: Response notes that many other values in the interval, such as 3 or 8, are also plausible, so exactly 5 is not shown.
criteria.fix: A plausible value is not a proven value; point out that other values in the interval remain plausible.

parts.prompt: A principal claims that Method A gives a mean exam score that is more than 10 points higher than Method B, that is, μA − μB > 10. Does the interval support this claim? Explain.

criteria.text: States that the interval does not support the claim, because 10 is greater than every value in the interval (the upper limit is 9.7).
criteria.evidence: Response answers no and cites that the upper limit 9.7 is below 10.
criteria.fix: Compare the claimed threshold with the limits; if the whole interval is below 10, the claim of more than 10 is not supported.

item.model_answer:
(a) Yes. The interval (2.1, 9.7) does not contain 0, so 0 is not a plausible value for the true difference, and there is convincing evidence of a difference in mean exam score. Every value in the interval is positive for A minus B, so Method A has the higher mean score.

(b) The claim is consistent with the interval because 5 is between 2.1 and 9.7, so 5 is a plausible value. The interval does not establish that the difference is exactly 5, because many other values in the interval, such as 3 or 8, are also plausible.

(c) No. The upper limit of the interval is 9.7, so every plausible value of μA − μB is less than 10. The interval does not support the claim that Method A is more than 10 points higher.
item.verification_python:
lo, hi = 2.1, 9.7
assert not (lo < 0 < hi) and lo > 0
assert lo < 5 < hi
assert hi < 10
print('ALL_CHECKS_PASSED')
